This rejection is respectfully traversed. Applicant has amended Claims 1, 2, 5 and 14 to ensure the proper limitations. Accordingly, Applicant respectfully requests withdraw of the rejection to these claims and respectfully submits that the scope thereof has not been limited in light of the subject amendment.
Claims 1-9 and 11-15 stand rejected under 35 U.S.C. §102(a)(1) as being anticipated by Rao et al. (US Pat Pub No. 20190110754 Al).
Claim 10 stands rejected under 35 U.S.C. §G103 as being unpatentable over Rao in view of Coleman et al. (U.S. Pat Pub. No. 20190113973 Al).
These rejections are respectfully traversed.

In making a rejection under 35 U.S.C. @ 102, the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit has stated: "For a prior art reference to anticipate a claim, it must disclose all of the limitations of the claim, arranged or combined in the same way as in the claim." Win. Wrigley Jr. Co. V. Cadbury Adams USA LLC, 683 F.3d 1356, 1361, 103 USPQ2d 1130, 1133 (Fed. Cir. 2012) (internal citations omitted). The Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit has also stated,

We thus hold that unless a reference discloses within the four corners of the document not only all of the limitations claimed but also all of the limitations arranged or combined in the same way as recited in the claim, it cannot be said to prove prior invention of the thing claimed and, thus, cannot anticipate under
Net MoneyIN Inc. V VeriSign Inc., 88 USPQ2d 1751, 1759-1760 (Fed. Cir. 2008) (emphasis added).

Independent claim 1 and dependent claims 2-9 and 11-15 are rejected as anticipated by Rao. Rao is directed to a system and methods for diagnosing and monitoring neurological disorders in a patient using an artificial intelligence based system. See Rao abstract. Rao further discloses that the system provides useful programming recommendations for medical devices implanted in a patient, and that such implanted medical devices include deep brain stimulation (DBS) devices. See Rao paragraph [0029], lines 1-3 and 6-8. Further, Rao discloses that neurostimulation devices are medical devices that deliver electrical current to specific regions of the brain or other parts of the nervous system for a therapeutic effect. See Rao paragraph [0029], lines 1-3. Regardless, in the embodiments disclosed in Rao, a deep brain stimulation (DBS) device is implanted in the patient's brain or nervous system, and the brain or nervous system is stimulated with electrical current.

Applicant respectfully submits, however, that independent claim 1 is not anticipated by Rao at least because independent claim 1 recites a neurological disorder decision support system for assisting an examiner to diagnose an examinee and to "the indication unit configured to issue an inquiry to the examinee according to a first indication signal and the interface unit configured for the examinee returning a response message according to the inquiry and acquiring a physiological characteristic related to the examinee to generate at least one of a physiological characteristic signal." The Applicant also wishes to emphasize that the present invention does not involve implanting a device into the patient's brain or nervous system. Accordingly, Rao does not anticipate independent claim 1 at least because Rao does not disclose all of the limitations recited therein at least because Rao discloses that a deep brain stimulation (DBS) device is implanted in the patient's brain or nervous system. Therefore, the skilled in the art would not refer to Rao when seeking to solve the problem of the present invention.
Further claims that depend from independent claim 1 include additional patentable subject matter.

For example, dependent claim 3 recites, "the input element providing at least one of an input basis data and a medical history data of the examinee." Rao does not disclose the technical features "providing at least one of an input basis data and a medical history data of the examinee." Rao discloses and illustrates features that use the built-in camera to record various facial expressions. See, Rao, paragraph [0104], lines 10-12.
Further, dependent claim 15 recites "...the diagnosis notification of the diagnosis module

is returned to the intelligent calculation module, and the intelligent calculation module is trained by the diagnosis notification based on at least one of the response message, the physiological characteristic signal, and the examination items". Applicant respectfully submits that Rao does not disclose dependent claim 15 by disclosing a diagnosis notification used to train the intelligent calculation module.

Further, Applicant respectfully submits that additional dependent claims, such as claim 10, is not anticipated or rendered obvious by Rao and Coleman. While Coleman discloses that the start and end points of the connections 302 described above (i.e., Software as a Service (SAAS) platform, paragraph [0321], line 7) can be configured to encrypt and decrypt data transmissions. However, Software as a Service (SAAS) is a software licensing and delivery model in which software is licensed on a subscription basis and centrally hosted, and SaaS is also known as on- demand software, web-based software, or web-hosted software. Coleman does not disclose that the Software as a Service (SAAS) platform is a transmission unit. While Coleman discloses the MD5 or SHA techniques, hash function MD5 and SHA are not encryption algorithms. The main reason why hash function MD5 and SHA and encryption are easily confused is that they are often used and discussed together, which leads to confusion over time. The two main points that distinguish hash function and encryption are as follows: encryption requires a key and can be decrypted to obtain the original plaintext (i.e., encryption is reversible), whereas hash function does not require a key and cannot be reversed to obtain the original input (i.e., hash function is irreversible). Furthermore, Coleman reveals that protocols such as secure HTTP (HTTPS) can be used to encrypt the transmission medium. However, Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure (HTTPS) is an extension of the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP). The primary motivations for HTTPS are to authenticate the site being accessed and to protect the privacy and integrity of the data being exchanged while it is in transit. It protects against man-in-the-middle attacks, and the bi- directional block cipher encryption of communications between a client and server protects communications from eavesdropping and tampering. Therefore, the skilled in the art would not refer to Coleman when seeking to solve the problem of the present invention.
In light of the foregoing, Applicant respectfully submits that the presently pending claims are in condition for allowance and that all of the outstanding rejections should be withdrawn.
